I wish there was mid-button... bc man... I would click it in a heartbeat. this game is extremely a pros and cons type of game. i love survival horror and where this does have the feel of that, it's ruined by oppressively taking you back to the beginning and losing all of your stuff, because of your death. Yup, it's a roguelite. That's right. The rooms change, the items change up and you lose all your stuff bc a monster camps you or u don't have enough healing. what's that? the combat is clunky? welcome to the 'clock tower' tag, because even that game had clunky combat, like all early 90's genre games. Now I know, i sound pessmestic, but it is a fun game if you go in with the mindset of NEVER dying. this what I did. I played it extremely safe and i'm now just in chp.3 with over 12 hrs... yes.... 12 hrs. lol honestly, imma finish it because I spent money on it (got it the day before it left early acess) and I'll probably enjoy it bc its gonna make me proud to know i havent died yet lol but dang... most fights aren't fun and sometimes the AI is really dumb. The game did not need to be roguelite, but here we are. anyways. The story...? its boring. i couldn't tell you whats happening. I just enjoy exploring and picking up items and stuff. There are notes to read, but they aren't interesting. idk... story falls flat when I'm just trying to survive XD something about a dream? or something... idk... and this is coming from a girl who LOVES lore in games. like shesh XD I say try it out for yourself ON SALE, if you are NOT a fan of roguelites. other then that, go wild and buy it. its worth it ^^ if you like to learn from your mistakes.

[b]Moonless Formless is a solo developer. What sorcery is this? Show him some love.[/b] I found out about Withering Rooms from Punchy's GDQ speedrun and I'm forever thankful to him. It's a horror metroidvania with procedural elements, I guess? And also a profound ARPG if you consider late Castlevania games as such. Stylistically, WR possesses traits of Sanitarium, Resident Evil, Silent Hill, and American McGee's Alice. Still in a league of its own, it bleeds profusely over the world it animates. You wake up in a corrupted Dream as a girl with bad posture, a clinical patient named Nightingale. A silent child in a screeching night with no end. The Dream isn't an evil phenomenon like Elm Street, only a violated miracle comprised of looping incorporeal processes. Bubbling with cruel ideas, the setting goes balls-to-the-wall, incorporating character-driven Lovecraftian sci-fi about human vices, trans-dimensional interpretation, and cycles of abuse. Defying thematic cohesiveness, the game invents its own theme of chaotic insanity. The setting takes root in Aztec culture and Byzantine mazes, all wrapped up in 1900s clinical horror. Washing away the meaning of things, burrowed deep within the heart of the Dream is the Curse. Its spiffing scorn permeates the grimy scenes of eclectic depravity. Being its guest, you shall burn alive, dredge knee-deep in poison sludge, and get eviscerated with a rusty sickle. So far, the Dream is unique to Mostyn House, which went from being a country retreat to a cholera clinic, then our trap - the asylum. Swarming with monsters and secret passages, the Lament Configuration twists itself each night on all layers of unreality. While the real-world bodies of its comatose explorers rot in beds, becoming nightmare creatures. Death in this existential deadlock is a fluke, your real body rots all the same. The suffering is tangible yet normalised. You won't see empathy from the desensitised factions, conflicting in a crackhouse world. Most inhabitants whose minds are still intact only push you around. By doing their bidding, and by your will, the Dream shapes into 4 endings. Its pliant nature isn't fully reflected in the game's randomiser. It's more of a theme. The overall map structure shifts slightly, it mostly impacts monster placement and loot. This could get monotonous if not for the constant growth. Initially, you get a few floors to roam, a lame Overlook's hedge maze. Then the world blows up, sprawls, endlessly choking on its own trauma, and protrudes its entrails further, with shortcuts, pits to jump into, sights to see. Dilapidated backgrounds bathe in crispy lighting, the visuals are explicit and raw, overtly Satanic, with slick animations and stark enemy designs stimulating the ultra-violence. When the Curse meter rises, reality peels off with it. Walls bleed, dressers turn sacks of spasming meat. Oppressive ambience, unnerving giggles, hidden chests, and panic-inducing hallucinations ensue! Alas, you won't be as amused when the meter fills. A massive chunk of Curse Rot damage suddenly hitting my face during an odd fight was the main cause of my strokes. [quote]"Janie says we're all such a crush of want, half-mad with loss We're violated in our sleep & we weep & we toss & we turn & we burn, we're hypnotised, we're cross-eyed We're pimped, we're b#tched, we're told such monstrous lies Janie wakes up & she says: we’re gonna have a real cool time tonite!" — Nick Cave[/quote] [h3]By Hook or by Crook[/h3] Panting, you scour around the mansion and its outskirts like a mouse, appearing from behind wardrobes and disappearing in mirrors. A bottom-feeder's min-max involves more than leaving a tart for later. The early power creep lies in discovering blood altars and travel points, slotting your item wheels with explosives along the way. Bring people's organs to blood altars to remember valuable items, build your permanent arsenal step by step. Death takes all that is forgotten, so embrace the "use it or lose it" mindset for resources and consumables. And there's no reason to grind. The game is separated into 4 chapters with progressively better loot in corpses and furniture. When you uncover most fast-travel mirrors, death recovery takes mere minutes. As long as you're running somewhere terrible, you make progress. I think running is better than the local stealth system. You can crouch under a table, but I only used it to evade shots and charges. Let the bodies hit the floor. Everyone's mortal, lootable, and the killing feels great! Granted, combat tends to go out of hand. One moment I'm on my merry way when, in a second, my army of knight armour and human-sized dolls gets incinerated by an SS flamethrower hulk. Next time, holding a Bible and a scythe, blindfolded, you pump a Byzantine titan full of paralytic agent. An axeman curses you in Greek while a witch of Salem giggles in the corner. Toss a grenade, slash her face, shotgun the Greek. Swap to the camera! Flash a ghost, run, get jumped by a nurse with a necrosis needle, roll, fireball, run outta the room to get sandwiched between a stone eye and a body bag slug! Still can't wake up. But can bulk up! WR's wide array of customisation options begins in its progression system. To level up your stats, initially, you offer organs to a witch. Or should you use a machine to harden your body with organ grease instead? Later, infuse yourself with ancient blood you found on a dusty skeleton, why not? It's more simple than it looks. The system constantly shifts like a dream, but it's intuitive and impactful. The stats should be familiar to everyone. Vigour, poise, resistances, curse tolerance, luck, perception, that useless inner light, and more... there’s room for self-expression. I went full-luck procs with a drop of vampirism, effortlessly facetanking all enemies and bosses by the end. I had to get crafty to make it work in NG+, but the level reset is free, you see. Consider this: the "rebirth" involves tearing off Nightingale flesh chunk by chunk, then reattaching it for whichever build you desire. Meanwhile, without any such requirements, the agreeable gear system provides a lion's share of your stats and important transformational effects. There's a heap of swords and whips to try on almost a hundred enemy types, each sporting a set of cheeky moves imbued with status effects. But you're spoiled for counters. Choose your synergetic dresses and rings with care, fashionably swapping outfits according to the situation at hand. Cursed or not, it's still a dream, so your drips can be as outrageous as you want. WR is pregnant with gunslinger hats, golden armour, and vampire tuxedos. It even has... 2 guns. But it's a classic combo - a revolver and a pump-action. Stab or pump, you have to be quick, aim accurately, and self-bandage timely. Staying lucid to pepper the crowd with acid jars and fireworks in-between. What else? The puzzles are clever. [h3]What Sorcery[/h3] Withering Rooms is obviously the fruit of many sleepless nights. I was bewitched and couldn't play anything else. Not until I was done enjoying melting every face available, exhausting every dialogue option with those I couldn't melt. I took their plights personally, which is a testament to the abnormal writing of this game. The visuals you can see, but that part is the jack in the box I can't convey without spoilers. I would never list to you all the intricacies forming this spectacular danse macabre anyway. In my case, it effortlessly eclipsed all competition for 2 weeks. Upon completion, I went for the NG+. Hard as nails, with a dress made of star meat and a sparkly sword, it was so different! I still prefer ending C, though. You may think differently, but you'll get involved to your ears. Because Withering Rooms is thoughtful, polished, well-balanced. It's mad as a Hatter and it's a barrel o' fun. [b]Tl;dr:[/b] Really cool concept let down by artificial difficulty. [b]Pros:[/b] + Creepy atmosphere + Good soundtrack + Interesting story and characters + You can get hints on the game website [b]Cons:[/b] - Unresponsive controls/clunky character - Too many enemies in later chapters - Too easy to become stun-locked - No i-frames in your dodge unless you're willing to pay a cost which screws you over as a spellcaster. Pretty much all defensive items have this cost except for shields which have durability. - Even basic enemies can have too much health [b]Closing Thoughts:[/b] I ended up making it to chapter 3 and stopping because it just got too frustrating. It never feels like you get any stronger because once you get something new or level up, all the enemies basically have countermeasures or are unaffected by it or there are just so many of them in a room that you get stun-locked if you try to do anything. Maybe if your character wasn't so clunky this might be more enjoyable. Clearly I'm the outlier here if recent reviews are anything to go by but people also liked Sekiro and I thought that was the worst of the Fromsoft games.

I cast a decoy spell, then dodge roll behind a shambling monstrosity and beat its head in with a lead pipe. Then I run out a nearby door and slap it with an explosive arcane trap as I pass, killing the backup that stupidly lumbers after me after seeing what I did to the back of its friend's skull. I loot their corpses for plants to turn into paralysing agents and acid bombs, then re-equip my Norse shield for the next fight. My frilly blue dress is stained with blood and the rings on my fingers make me itch for violence. The lady in my peripheral vision laughs at me again. I don't mind. ---- All is well with the witch leader who incinerated me on sight when I first got here. The beef has been squashed, and I now cordially toss her all my spare change and rotting limbs, and in return she makes my bones into steel. There's still a big, lumbering problem in the dining hall, who is apparently so juiced that it takes three paralysing grenades to even make him flex his traps. He has dashed my skull into the nice shiny floors a few too many times. Along with that, if I even slightly approach his buddy Mozart while dodging his swings, the guy immediately stops playing Serenade No. 13, stands up, and starts striding towards me like I punched his grandma. I can't even see him unless he is reflected in a mirror, I have no way to harm him, and the big man still scares me. ♥♥♥♥ the dining hall. I need to become one with the mirror. ---- Later, I exit the witch basement, so high off bad juju and spirit dust that local furniture is floating through the ceiling and being replaced by bloodied, caged mannequins. I crawl through a hole in the mirror to reach Nowhere, a serene, starry ether plane where business is booming. I sell photographs of spirits to a man who can't remember his name. In return, he deals me ghostly trinkets, and loads of cash money american dollars. You see, I've found my calling in this dream, not even four nights in. Ghoul hustling. I'm a dealer of the damned. A haunt huckster. A poltergeist peddler. A shade smuggler. And as this bandaged junkie keeps satisfying his memory-fix off my photographs, I get richer and richer, AND I get free passage throughout the mansion with the mirror's portal network. If I use any more magic at this point, my soul will rot from the inside out though, so I'm kind of stuck with my trusty pipe, and that's bad news for the rest of the mansion. ---- I'm still in a dream, snake eater. I've been popping flash bulbs into most spirits in the house, and getting profit in earnest to keep me going strong throughout the rest of the house, letting me explore more. The paranoid butcher in the basement that was hired to dissect bodies now dissects bodies for fun. Despite this man openly confessing to me that he kidnaps children to take apart in the dream to be a better surgeon IRL, I continue to talk to him. He goes berserk at the drop of a hat, and after many throwing knives, invisible witch branch sucker punches, and clutch closet dodges, he goes down. I now mix his blood in the sacrifice altar so that I can keep my trusty lead pipe with me next time I mess up and wake up in here. My next destination is the hedge maze outside the house. A devout man in a Crusader's helmet tells me not to associate with witches or their spells lest I be cast down in the eyes of the Lord. Little does he know, I'm so high off the Coven's arcane bath salts that the hedges around me are made of meat. Despite this, I do in fact carry a bible, and Matthew 4:10 is my greatest weapon against the paranormal next to flash photography. I ignore him, he's a hater. I catch a child rummaging through the body of one of my kills. One of the Wretch's little scavengers again. I crack it over the head with my pipe, and it goes limp. My turf, my business, my loot. That should send him a message. My vision blurs constantly, so I drink more coffee. --- While I shoulder-check my way through my fellow asylum patients and rummage through dressers, I'm finding more out about Mostyn House, and the dream that keeps me trapped rotting in my bed in the waking world, while I fight for my life in a shared consciousness with other patients. Alfred Mostyn, a Welsh coal mogul, had this house built as a country home, and then died from pneumonia along with his daughter. Before the final member of the family, Peter, also passed, he gifted this house to an American physician and his daughter Margaret... the same woman who's been guiding me through this nightmare, and one of my few allies here. Hang on, if she owned this place along with her father, what's she doing wading through the dreamscape with the asylum patients? Before I can return to the foyer to talk to Margaret and catch myself up on her story, the floor begins to shake as footsteps rapidly approach. The tallest chambermaid I have ever seen sprints towards me, and proceeds to beat me over the head with a candelabra. As I back away to apply first aid, I am jumped by a skeletal apparition. Before I can pull out my lens piece and escalate gang violence with a snapshot, it sprays me with so much ghost coke that my tolerance gives out, and my skin crumbles into ash. ---- I wake up in the bed again, my hand already gripping my lead pipe and camera. I have lost everything else, but that's fine, for what else need I remember, in a place like this? My memory is sharp, and my friends are just a mirror away. I know my way around this mansion, even as it shifts to disorient, and I will build my empire again. I have abominations to concuss, witchcraft to study, and a story of bloody tragedy to unravel. ---- I'd recommend this game if you're interested by what you saw in the trailer. I promise it is even more than it seems. This game mixes so many genres and it all blends, introducing all of its mechanics to you at a reasonable pace and allowing you to make the most of them as you scrounge for resources to figure out strategies to deal with each section of the house. The combat is definitely janky, but I found that an enjoyable challenge to work around, and as you get more familiar with your weapons, items and rings, you find ways to circumvent obstacles and tip encounters to your favor. The atmosphere is downright oppressive at times, especially with the well-done sanity mechanic, which leaves you toeing the line of madness to reveal hidden secrets and benefits from being at a high curse level. The game rewards a sharp eye and frequent checks of your inventory, map and notes. The soundtrack and environments are surreal and you never feel fully safe. The game also opens up as you play, with a massive map, an arena mode, minigames, a NG+ hook, and a smaller roguelike microcosm inside the game, which is fitting considering the story. Speaking of which, the story goes places far beyond the initial 'escape the house and dream' goal, with a lot to say on ethics, industry, and surprisingly, abuse. The worldbuilding is surprisingly deep, and the many notes you find throughout your playthrough help piece together how the world operates and how people have adapted to the setting. I only wish there was a wiki for the game where I could see all the characters' dialogue to better piece together the history of Mostyn House and the many people and factions inhabiting it, though I guess the NG+ is there for a reason. Not only is the game replayable with the vast amount of gear and playstyle options you have at your disposal, but multiple endings and a fresh view on the world will change the way you see many characters from start to finish. I plan to replay it at some point, but I need a breather for now. Make no mistake, this is a fully finished game with a lot of love put into it, which is more than many triple A games can say for this price. A worthy tribute to classic adventure games, and a solid entry that stands up well on its own. Hats off to Moonless Formless for one of the most engrossing games I've played this year.

This is not a 2d Dark Souls or even souls-like. Withering Rooms is more like a very simple metroidvania in which you find the necessary item to move forward and do just that. There aren't really "builds" that you can do, you just switch for the better weapon (the one that deals more damage) and that's it. There's some magic but I found it kinda lackluster. The meat of the game, combat, feels very stiff and is not fun. Whack, roll, whack, roll, and the character feels janky. Withering Rooms might've been a decent game in a world where there is no competition in this genre. Here it's just not enough in any area.

The game makes a lot of hay about all these girls sent to an asylum for misbehaving but once they're there and introduced to a wondrous dream where they can't die and magic is real they almost all decide to become psychotic witches and start murdering people. Whatever misbehavior was an old school euphemism for, I suspect people were right to send girls to an asylum for that. Also the back half of the game is absolutely bloated and drawn out with enemies with equally bloated stats but you can always leg it to a merchant and will always have enough money to restock medkits and consumables so it just feels like the soulless ARPG drudgery of shooting at a big fat health bar and mashing the health potion button whenever you get wrecked all just lasting WAY too long. It's not like I have a tactic available to me to meaningfully mitigate damage anyway. Even the ones you could pretend worked would just draw the fight out longer and cost more than chomping medkits. And the roguelite part is a wash. It was supposed to make horror game pathing no longer a solved problem but now it's just an even longer, even more boring Dark Souls corpse run spread across an entire level collecting your old power back piecemeal before you can start killing again. Just to add one more thing: A lot of people are expecting Souls here but the game does not want to give you the Souls dodge. You CANNOT just mash attack and roll through enemy swings here. You aren't fast enough. The dev does not want you doing that for free (And this isn't a bad choice but it is a confounding one for several reviewers). You MUST use a resource or some other trick to try to dance like that, which means there is a hard limit to it. And for several reasons beyond just that, melee combat is not viable long term after around act 1.

生存恐怖+2d血源+rougelite，这可真是太好玩了 这真是一款极挑受众的[strike]缝合怪[/strike]厨力释放独游，毕竟你既要能忍受魂游极致残疾的人物性能，又要能享受游戏前期的生存恐怖氛围、与死亡重来的轻度肉鸽，还要对复古解谜有着不小的热情。但很不幸的是本人满足了以上一切，于是该作就切切实实地击中了我的好球区。 毕竟本作的tag实在是让人难以想象如何能拼凑成一款游戏的，那么通俗点来说，这就是一个极致复古的钟楼+蔷薇守则+2d血源，再给你缝一点零的拍照、生化寂静岭的解谜与怪物、层层恐惧的场景。还不够？那再加点肉鸽！玩到中期，看到各式各样莫名熟悉的要素出现，我只能直呼好家伙。但与此同时，又不得不慨叹本作缝的是那么巧妙，且那么迷人。 说两点极其优秀的设计： —— [u][b]诅咒条的设计[/b][/u]。使用道具法术、被幽灵攻击等，都会积累诅咒条。而诅咒条的积累会使目所能及的环境产生变化（类似寂静岭的里世界），致使你既能看到本无法看到的隐藏门，又会不断被里世界的秽物侵扰。但诅咒条涨满反而会造成异常持续扣血。这个出自血源灵视又高于灵视的设计成为了本作游玩的重心之一，如何管理诅咒条进行战斗和环境交互也极大地提升了游玩乐趣。 —— [u][b]循序渐进的碎片化叙事、配上维多利亚的美术与生存恐怖氛围[/b][/u]。这个被血源证明过是天作之合的搭配终于找到了它理想的传承者。旅程途中遇到的各式各样npc、都只会告诉你他们视角中故事的冰山一角，而在环境叙事、与抽丝剥茧逐步揭开世界观时，才会有理解每个人物动机的醍醐味。这种由强叙事驱动的探索欲，已经很久没有在如今这些“罐头类魂”游戏中出现了。 当然，还有一些不尽如人意的： —— [u][b]丰富的武器法术装备种类，但手感极其糟糕且僵硬的战斗[/b][/u]。魂游下水道般的动作系统甚至少了一个维度，3d变2d的结果就是：回合制变得更加回合制，残疾人变得更加残疾人。即便游戏给了防滚滑硬的反制手段，却因为2d、残疾性能、和巨大的动作前后摇，实际根本无法和怪物立回。绝大多数情况下战斗会衍变成近战举盾回合制、原地对砍，远程控制距离施法/射击。在中后期BD成型后更是轮椅复读，无脑是真无脑，无趣也是真无趣。 —— [u][b]中后期大量回血道具与资源的溢出，让肉鸽要素不复存在，难度直线下降[/b][/u]。当然肉鸽在本作中本就不太突出，实际上死亡后重置的也只有未记忆的道具、商人出售物品、与场景房间布局次序罢了。但是在中后期有二三十格记忆格、与无限补给的恢复品、甚至还有吸血这种逆天词条后，人物可以直接凭借数值碾压一切。从而不仅仅是难度，恐怖氛围也会被消解。 ++++ 独特的游戏类型与机制 +++ 极具质感的美术风格、叙事结构与世界观 ++ 优秀的音乐与氛围营造 ++ 种类丰富的武器道具法术、与流派式玩法 ++ 种类丰富的怪物，体量足够的地图流程与解谜 = 毫无用武之地的躲藏 = 存在刷刷刷要素，但并非必要 - BD成型后的难度下降、与恐怖氛围削减 - 抵达二周目结局的粗暴数值提升 - 无中文 -- 僵硬糟糕的战斗手感 爷爷你要的血源精神续作有了，只不过是2d独游 9/10

之前因为这游戏的近战太过坐牢，导致死了东西都掉光了，怒而直接删掉游戏。 最近重新拾起这款游戏，尝试了魔法路线，发现这游戏的整套机制就是为了魔法而存在了，开荒不要太爽了。 这里介绍一下我的开荒打法，非常适合手残的新手玩家。 前期尽快买到【学徒烛台】，这是所有前期武器中攻击距离最远的。后面直接换成【新人的蜡烛台】，有了这把神器你就可以远程爆杀敌人。 然后找到女巫把法力的上限升上去，我是前10点全加到法力上面，后面再抬【咒语伤害】。 接着捡到【诅咒类】或【咒语类】的戒指立马装上，主要看【诅咒忍耐】、【咒语反噬】、【咒语伤害】三个词条，第一个增加法力上限，第二个减少法力消耗，最后那个增加你的伤害，衣服帽子护符同理。【诅咒伤害】不用管，装备成型后敌人基本打不到你，更不可能对你造成【诅咒伤害】。 【蜡烛】买满，一个才两块钱，巨便宜。【树枝】买满，法力消耗完了之后就开【树枝】开【蜡烛】原地回蓝，可以应对一些BOSS狂追你不给你回蓝的场景，另外【娃娃】也可以吸引注意力。 回血瓶基本不用专门去做，如果怕血少暴毙就多做【护甲卷轴】，这个卷轴开了效果是一直在的，可以抵消任何物理魔法伤害，而且你【咒语伤害】越高，护甲加得越多。 最后再整个物理减伤高的护盾，用来抵御敌人打枪丢刀子这些远程攻击。 整完上面这套，你基本就可以在游戏里面横着走了！ 最后大力推荐汉化去搜游侠那个LMAO汉化包，翻译得比机翻好一万倍。

I would strongly encourage anyone curious about Withering Rooms to first try the demo—it's the most direct way to see if you’ll click with it. That said, the full release has some rough edges worth noting. The most significant issue I encountered came in Chapter 2, where the game began crashing frequently—often after killing a few enemies. Thanks to the game’s auto-save when entering new rooms, I never lost much progress, but I still experienced several crashes. These interruptions quickly drained my will to keep playing, which is a shame because there are moments where this game really shines. Another point you’ll notice even in the demo: while you can technically play melee, the game isn’t balanced around it. Melee feels weak and resource-draining, especially early on. Most encounters will push you toward throwing projectiles, casting spells, sneaking, and avoiding damage entirely. Equipment exists to make melee more viable, but in my experience, it never became satisfying. That out of the way, this is still an incredible project for a solo developer. The atmosphere, writing, and music all work beautifully together to make the asylum an engaging place to explore. I especially appreciate the stylistic touches: in-game letters use different fonts, characters’ dialogue is styled to reflect their tone, and conversations feature subtle camera zooms that emphasize certain lines. Outside of the story, the game offers exploration, puzzles, and combat. Exploration is easily one of its strongest aspects—thanks to the intricate house design, the secrets hidden within, and the gear you can uncover. Finding something that gives you an advantage feels significant. Puzzles are handled well, too. The developer even provides a website with solutions for those stuck, and there’s an in-game item that can skip puzzles (re-purchasable at a higher price). I don’t usually enjoy puzzles in games, but I liked them here. Combat, however, is where the experience falters. Enemies hit hard, inflict status effects quickly, and have bloated health pools. Melee damage feels pitiful, which forces reliance on spells and projectiles. Spells require crafting and come with “spell toll” damage if overused, while projectiles have limited ammo. This creates a repetitive loop: buy supplies from a merchant, explore a few rooms, run out, and repeat. Bosses follow the same pattern—they soak damage but do benefit from a checkpoint candle that allows you to retry fights without replaying long stretches. I think players who view combat here more as a puzzle will get more out of it, but mechanically it feels janky and drawn-out. The “Danger” mechanic, which gives you a healing chance at 1 HP, helps a bit, and the “Narrative” difficulty mode dramatically reduces enemy health and damage—but that mode made the game far too easy and dull for me. As someone who enjoys combat-heavy games, I found neither difficulty satisfying, especially when victories sometimes led straight into another crash. If you value exploration, a cohesive and interesting story, and can look past mechanical flaws, Withering Rooms might still captivate you. But if you play primarily for tight, satisfying combat, this game probably isn’t for you.

87/100 Just finished the game 100%, all achievements and wanted to leave a brief review. You play as a young witch who in the beginning is trying to break free from her captors but quickly learn that there are many more people imprisoned in the Asylum. Considering the fact that Withering Rooms was made by ONE developer only, I was very positively suprised by the overall game's quality. Overall phenomenal game, especially considering the teams size. + Game starts very simple but gets more and more intense & difficult the longer you play, preventing the game from becoming too boring in the long run + Overall good graphics & stable performance + Very diverse soundtracks, every area which features different rooms has its own music + Story is impossible to predict outside of a few lore details/hints you can find + Multiple decisions you can make during the game which impact the story outcome slightly + Very easy to understand combat system with simple inputs + 3 different combat playstyles to choose from (melee, magic, gun weapons) + Many different small and large enemies, each with unique strenghts & weaknesses + Multiple endings with one secret ending to chose from + New Game Plus features lots of NEW content and expanded story which answers most open questions left from the main story - Personally wished for more available weapons during the mid game, especially for magic users - craftable spells didn't feel rewarding enough - The game was tons of fun until the very second you die and spill out your entire inventory, part of the genre & part of the game but still frustrating - No spoilers but the main story might even be too complex for many to properly understand
